definition: The tendency of a program to access memory addresses close to those it used recently.
wrongs: The tendency to reuse the exact same address many times in a short interval.
A cache policy that updates main memory on every store.
A page-table bit that marks a page as recently referenced.
why: Nearby addresses are often needed together, so a cache fetches a whole line rather than a single word.
example: A loop reads pixels left to right, so the next pixel often arrives in the line fetched for the current one.
scenario: A scan of an array misses less often after the line size grows from 4 bytes to 64 bytes. Which locality does the larger line exploit?
scenarioWhy: Consecutive elements share a cache line, so one miss supplies several later sequential accesses.

definition: The tendency of a program to reference the same memory location again soon after using it.
wrongs: The tendency to access addresses that sit next to the last address used.
A guarantee that every instruction finishes in one clock cycle.
The time a block spends waiting in a write buffer.
why: A value used recently is likely to be needed again, so keeping it in a fast cache avoids another trip to memory.
example: A loop accumulator is read and written on every iteration, so its latest value stays in a register or in L1.
scenario: A tight loop updates one accumulator a million times and almost never misses on that variable. Which locality explains the hits?
scenarioWhy: The accumulator is reused immediately, so the copy already in cache satisfies the later accesses.

definition: A memory access that finds its data in the cache and returns it without using the next memory level.
wrongs: A memory access that must be fetched from main memory because no valid copy is cached.
A store that updates main memory and the cache in the same cycle by policy.
A translation that misses in the TLB and starts a page-table walk.
why: A valid line whose tag matches the requested address already holds the data the CPU needs.
example: The second load of a stack variable in one function returns from L1 in a few cycles.
scenario: A load finds a valid tag match in the selected cache set. How is that access classified?
scenarioWhy: A valid matching tag means the requested block is already resident in the cache.

definition: A memory access whose block is not valid in the cache, so the block must be fetched from a lower level.
wrongs: A memory access satisfied entirely from a valid matching cache line.
A branch whose direction was guessed correctly.
A disk transfer performed entirely by a DMA controller.
why: Without a valid matching line, the cache cannot supply the data and must fill from the next level.
example: The first reference to a cold array element brings a line in from DRAM.
scenario: The tag compare fails for every way in the set. What must happen before the load can complete?
scenarioAnswer: The block is fetched from the next memory level
scenarioWrongs: The data is returned from a matching line
scenarioWhy: No valid tag matched the address, so the block is absent and has to be filled.

definition: A cache miss on the first reference to a block that has never been loaded.
wrongs: A miss caused because the working set is larger than the cache.
A miss caused because several live blocks map to the same set.
A miss caused by writing a dirty line back to memory.
why: A block that has never been touched cannot already be cached, so its first reference misses.
example: After a cold start, the first instruction fetch of main misses even though the cache still has empty lines.
scenario: An empty cache misses on the first touch of every new block, and a larger cache does not remove those misses. Which miss type is that?
scenarioWhy: Those blocks were never resident, so the first reference misses regardless of capacity or associativity.

definition: A cache miss that occurs because the working set does not fit, even if the cache is fully associative.
wrongs: A miss on the very first reference to a block that was never cached.
A miss caused only by two blocks colliding in one direct-mapped line.
A miss caused by a stale translation in the TLB.
why: A fully associative cache of the same size would still have to evict a live block, so the miss is due to capacity.
example: A matrix multiply whose working set is 2 MB keeps thrashing a 32 KB L1 cache however the lines are mapped.
scenario: Misses remain after a direct-mapped cache is replaced by a fully associative cache of the same size. Which miss type remains?
scenarioWhy: Full associativity removes mapping conflicts, so leftover misses mean the working set exceeds the cache.

definition: A miss caused when too many live blocks map to one set even though other lines in the cache are unused.
wrongs: A miss that remains even in a fully associative cache of the same size.
A miss on the first reference to a block that was never cached.
A miss caused by two cores writing the same shared variable.
why: The placement rule confines the block to a set that is already full of other live blocks.
example: Two hot arrays whose addresses share a direct-mapped index evict each other on every iteration.
scenario: A direct-mapped cache thrashes on two blocks, but a fully associative cache of the same size hits on both. Which miss was removed?
scenarioWhy: The blocks fit in the cache, but direct-mapped placement forced them into the same line.

definition: A cache in which each memory block may occupy only one line, selected by index bits.
wrongs: A cache in which a block may occupy any line in the cache.
A cache in which a block may occupy any of several lines inside one set.
A cache that stores no tags because every address hits.
why: The index selects exactly one candidate line, so placement uses a single tag comparison.
example: Index bits of an address always select line 47, and only that line may hold the block.
scenario: A block may reside in exactly one line, and a second block with the same index replaces it. Which organization is this?
scenarioWhy: One index maps to one line, so any other block with that index must replace the resident block.

definition: A cache that groups lines into sets and lets a block occupy any line inside its one set.
wrongs: A cache that lets a block occupy any line in the whole cache.
A cache that assigns each block to exactly one line.
A cache that has no tags and compares only the block offset.
why: The index selects a set of several ways, which needs more comparators but removes some mapping conflicts.
example: In a four-way cache, four blocks that share an index can reside together, and a fifth must replace one.
scenario: Each address maps to a set of four lines, and those four tags are compared in parallel. Which organization is this?
scenarioWhy: Four ways are searched in the indexed set, which is four-way set associativity.

definition: A cache in which a memory block may be placed in any line, with every tag compared together.
wrongs: A cache in which each block maps to exactly one line.
A cache that uses an index and never compares more than one tag.
A cache that writes every store straight to DRAM.
why: There is no index restriction, so a block is rejected only when every line holds something more useful.
example: A 64-entry TLB compares all 64 tags and may hold any 64 recent page translations.
scenario: A small cache compares the incoming tag with every line and may store the block in any free line. Which organization is this?
scenarioWhy: Any line is a legal home for the block, so every tag must be compared.

definition: A write policy that updates the cache line and the next memory level on every store.
wrongs: A policy that updates only the cache and writes memory when a dirty line is evicted.
A policy that drops the store when the line is absent and does not update memory.
A policy that loads a missing block on a read but never accepts stores.
why: Memory sees each new value immediately, so a line does not need a dirty bit for correctness.
example: Every store to a frame buffer updates L1 and is also sent onward to DRAM.
scenario: Stores never set a dirty bit because main memory is updated on every store. Which write policy is in use?
scenarioWhy: Memory is kept current on each store, so eviction does not need to write a dirty line.

definition: A write policy that updates only the cache and copies a line to memory later if that line is dirty.
wrongs: A policy that writes main memory on every store.
A policy that caches instructions and never accepts data stores.
A policy that invalidates a line on every load.
why: Repeated stores hit in the cache, and memory traffic waits until a dirty line is evicted.
example: A loop stores to one line a thousand times, and DRAM is written once when that dirty line is replaced.
scenario: A line is marked dirty on a store, and DRAM is written only when that line is replaced. Which policy is this?
scenarioWhy: The dirty bit records that memory is stale and must be updated if the line is evicted.

definition: A write-miss policy that loads the missing block into the cache and then performs the store.
wrongs: A write-miss policy that updates lower memory and does not load the block into the cache.
A read policy that bypasses the cache on every load.
A policy that allocates a physical page on a TLB hit.
why: Bringing the block in lets later reads and writes to that block hit in the cache.
example: A store to a cold stack slot misses, the line is filled from DRAM, and the byte is then updated in cache.
scenario: A store misses, the cache fetches the block, and only then updates the word. Which write-miss policy is this?
scenarioWhy: The missing block is allocated in the cache so the store can update the cached copy.

definition: The fixed-size block moved and stored as one cache entry, together with its tag and state bits.
wrongs: A single bit stored in a flip-flop inside the ALU.
The set of wires that carry only interrupt numbers.
A page-table entry that maps one virtual page.
why: The cache fills, hits, and evicts data in lines so one miss can serve several nearby addresses.
example: A 64-byte fill brings in sixteen 32-bit words after a miss on any byte in that aligned block.
scenario: A miss on one byte fetches 64 aligned bytes into the cache. What unit was transferred?
scenarioWhy: The cache fill size is one line, so the neighboring bytes in that aligned block come in together.

definition: A replacement rule that evicts the line in a set which has gone unused for the longest time.
wrongs: A rule that always evicts the line that was used most recently.
A rule that evicts a line chosen at random from the entire cache.
A rule that evicts only invalid lines and never a valid one.
why: Under temporal locality, the line unused the longest is the least likely to be needed soon.
example: In a two-way set, the way that was not touched on the previous hit is replaced on the next miss.
scenario: A two-way set holds blocks A and B. A was used more recently, and a miss needs a victim. Which block does LRU evict?
scenarioWhy: B has been unused longer than A, so least-recently-used replacement selects B.

definition: A technique that gives each process a private address space mapped onto physical memory and secondary storage.
wrongs: A small CPU cache that holds only the most recently used data line.
A bus that carries physical addresses from the processor to DRAM.
A disk layout that stripes blocks across drives with no redundancy.
why: Programs use virtual addresses, and hardware plus the operating system translate them so processes stay isolated.
example: Two processes both use address 0x400000, but those pages are mapped to different physical frames.
scenario: Each process appears to own a private address space that can be larger than installed RAM. Which mechanism provides that view?
scenarioWhy: Page translation gives each process its own addresses backed by frames and disk.

definition: A per-process structure that records which physical frame, if any, holds each virtual page.
wrongs: A cache of recent branch target addresses inside the fetch unit.
A list of dirty cache lines waiting to be written back.
A table of interrupt-handler addresses in a microcontroller.
why: The memory-management unit uses this table to turn a virtual page number into a frame number and permissions.
example: Virtual page 12 is marked present in frame 90, so addresses in that page translate using frame 90.
scenario: The MMU needs the frame number and permission bits for virtual page 40. Which structure supplies them?
scenarioWhy: The page table is the structure that maps virtual pages to frames and access rights.

definition: A small cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations that avoids a full page-table walk.
wrongs: A cache of data lines fetched from DRAM.
A buffer that holds stores until they commit to disk.
A predictor that guesses whether a branch is taken.
why: Translation is on the critical path of every memory access, so recent page-table entries are cached beside the MMU.
example: After the first load on a page, later loads on that page hit in the TLB and skip the multi-level walk.
scenario: A load's page is resident in RAM, but its translation is absent from the MMU cache, so a walk begins. What missed?
scenarioWhy: The page is already in memory, so this is a translation-cache miss rather than a page fault.

definition: An exception raised when a process references a virtual page that is not currently in physical memory.
wrongs: A TLB miss for a page that is already resident in RAM.
A cache miss that is filled from DRAM without involving the operating system.
A branch misprediction that flushes the pipeline.
why: The page-table present bit is clear, so the operating system must bring the page in or reject the access.
example: The first touch of a new heap page traps, and the operating system allocates a frame before retrying the instruction.
scenario: The present bit of the referenced page is clear and the instruction traps to the operating system. Which exception is this?
scenarioWhy: A clear present bit means the virtual page has no frame, so hardware cannot complete the reference.

definition: A policy that loads a page from secondary storage only when a reference to that page faults.
wrongs: A policy that copies every page of a program into RAM before the program starts.
A policy that pins all pages so they can never be evicted.
A policy that writes every store through to disk immediately.
why: Pages that are never touched consume neither a frame nor a transfer from disk.
example: A photo editor starts immediately, and a filter's code page is read from disk only when the user first applies that filter.
scenario: A process starts with no code pages resident, and each new page is read from disk on its first reference. Which policy is this?
scenarioWhy: Pages are fetched in response to faults rather than being loaded before execution begins.

definition: An organization that overlaps stages of several instructions, such as fetch, decode, execute, and writeback.
wrongs: A design that finishes one instruction completely before fetching the next.
A design that issues several instructions in one cycle to multiple functional units.
A buffer that retires instructions in a different order from program order.
why: While one instruction executes, another can be decoded and a third fetched, raising throughput toward one instruction per cycle.
example: On one clock edge, five instructions occupy the five stages of a classic pipeline.
scenario: The fetch of instruction 5 overlaps the execution of instruction 3. Which technique allows that overlap?
scenarioWhy: Different instructions occupy different stages at the same time, which is pipelining.

definition: A pipeline dependence in which an instruction needs a value that an earlier instruction has not yet written.
wrongs: A situation in which the next PC is unknown until a branch resolves.
A situation in which two instructions need the same hardware unit in one cycle.
A situation in which two cores lack a coherent copy of one block.
why: The consumer reads a register or memory location before the producer has made the new value visible.
example: An add writes r1 in writeback, but the next instruction reads r1 during decode, before that write.
scenario: Instruction 2 reads r3, which instruction 1 will write, but the write has not reached the register file. Which hazard is this?
scenarioWhy: The second instruction depends on a result that the first instruction has not yet produced.

definition: A pipeline delay that occurs because the next instruction address is unknown until a branch resolves.
wrongs: A delay caused because a source register has not yet been written.
A delay caused because two instructions need the only divider.
A delay caused by writing a dirty cache line back to DRAM.
why: Fetch cannot know which instruction follows until the branch condition and target are known.
example: After a conditional branch is fetched, the pipeline does not yet know whether to fetch the fall-through or the target.
scenario: Fetch stalls because a conditional branch has not yet produced the next PC. Which hazard is this?
scenarioWhy: The unresolved branch leaves the address of the next instruction unknown.

definition: A pipeline conflict in which two instructions need the same hardware resource in the same cycle.
wrongs: A conflict in which one instruction needs a result that is not yet written.
A conflict caused only by an unresolved branch target.
A conflict between two virtual pages that share one frame.
why: Overlapped instructions can collide when the machine has only one copy of a unit such as a memory port.
example: An instruction fetch and a data load both need the single memory port on the same clock, so one waits.
scenario: A load in the memory stage and an instruction fetch both need the only memory port this cycle. Which hazard is this?
scenarioWhy: The instructions are contending for one physical resource even though their data are independent.

definition: A bypass that sends a result from a later pipeline stage directly to an earlier stage that needs it.
wrongs: A stall that inserts a bubble until the register file is written.
A guess of whether a branch will be taken.
A map from architectural register names to physical registers.
why: The result already exists in a pipeline register before writeback, so a dependent instruction can use it immediately.
example: An add result leaving the ALU is fed to the next instruction's ALU input instead of waiting for the register write.
scenario: A dependent add uses the previous ALU result from the execute-memory pipeline register and does not stall. Which technique avoided the stall?
scenarioWhy: The bypass path supplied the result to the consumer before the register file was updated.

definition: A deliberate delay that holds an instruction and inserts a bubble until a hazard clears.
wrongs: A bypass that supplies a result without waiting for writeback.
A prediction used to keep fetching along a guessed branch path.
The eviction of the least recently used line in a set.
why: If a needed value or resource is not available and cannot be bypassed, the dependent instruction must wait.
example: The instruction after a load waits one cycle because the loaded data is not ready for the next ALU operation.
scenario: Decode freezes and a bubble is inserted because the next instruction needs a load result that is not yet available. What was inserted?
scenarioWhy: The consumer cannot proceed until the load data returns, so the hardware inserts a bubble.

definition: A guess, made before a branch resolves, of whether the branch is taken so that fetch can continue.
wrongs: A rule that every branch is taken and the fall-through path is never fetched.
A bypass of an ALU result to a dependent instruction.
A table that translates virtual page numbers into frames.
why: Waiting for the true next PC would stall fetch, so a likely path is fetched and later checked.
example: A backward loop branch is predicted taken after many taken outcomes, and fetch follows the loop body.
scenario: Fetch follows the loop body before the compare that controls the branch has finished. What supplied that direction?
scenarioWhy: The direction was chosen before the branch condition was known, which is prediction.

definition: A cache indexed by branch address that stores predicted target addresses of recent branches.
wrongs: A buffer of retired store data waiting to be written to DRAM.
A table of physical frames for every virtual page of a process.
A queue of instruction results waiting to commit in program order.
why: Fetch needs a predicted target in the same cycle it recognizes a branch, before decode computes that target.
example: The entry for a call supplies the callee address so the next fetch does not wait for the target calculation.
scenario: Fetch looks up the current PC and immediately obtains a predicted next PC for a branch. Which structure returned that PC?
scenarioWhy: A cache of branch targets indexed by the branch PC is a branch target buffer.

definition: Execution of instructions on a predicted path before that prediction is known to be correct.
wrongs: Execution that waits for every branch to resolve before fetching further instructions.
Execution of two processes at once on two separate cores.
Execution that writes architectural state before an instruction has been fetched.
why: The processor uses otherwise idle cycles on the predicted path and discards that work if the prediction was wrong.
example: Instructions after a predicted-taken branch run, then are squashed when the branch is actually not taken.
scenario: Instructions past a branch execute before its condition is known, and they are discarded when the guess is wrong. What is this called?
scenarioWhy: Work proceeded on a guess and was thrown away when the guess failed.

definition: A processor that can issue more than one instruction in the same cycle to multiple functional units.
wrongs: A processor that overlaps pipeline stages but issues only one instruction per cycle.
A processor that runs one instruction to completion before fetching another.
A chip with several cores that run separate threads.
why: Multiple issue uses instruction-level parallelism beyond the one-instruction-per-cycle limit of a scalar pipeline.
example: In one cycle an integer add is sent to the ALU while an independent load is sent to the memory unit.
scenario: In one cycle the processor issues an add and an independent load to two different units. Which organization is this?
scenarioWhy: Two instructions from the pipeline were issued in the same cycle, which is superscalar execution.

definition: Execution that starts an instruction when its operands are ready, even if an earlier instruction is still waiting.
wrongs: Execution that always runs instructions in exact program order.
Execution that issues only one instruction per cycle on one pipeline.
Execution that commits stores to memory before the instruction is decoded.
why: A stalled instruction should not block later independent instructions whose inputs are already available.
example: A cache-missing load waits, while a later add that does not use the loaded value executes and holds its result.
scenario: A load misses, and a later independent add executes before that load completes. Which policy allowed the add to run early?
scenarioWhy: The add ran before an earlier instruction finished because the add's own operands were ready.

definition: Mapping architectural registers onto a larger physical set so that each new write receives a fresh name.
wrongs: Bypassing an ALU result to the next instruction without assigning a new register.
Saving callee-saved registers on the stack during a function call.
Translating virtual addresses to physical frames.
why: A new physical register removes write-after-read and write-after-write hazards, which are not true data dependences.
example: Two adds both write architectural r1, but renaming assigns the results to physical registers p12 and p17.
scenario: A later add writes r1 while an earlier instruction still must read the old r1, and the add receives a new physical register. Which hazard is removed?
scenarioWhy: The new write uses a different physical register, so it does not overwrite the value the earlier reader still needs.

definition: A structure that holds results of instructions finished out of order until they can commit in program order.
wrongs: A cache of predicted branch target addresses.
A buffer that stores only dirty cache lines waiting for write-back.
The page table consulted on a TLB miss.
why: In-order commit keeps architectural state precise and lets wrongly speculated instructions be discarded.
example: An add finishes before an earlier load, and its result stays buffered until that load has committed.
scenario: An instruction has executed, but its result updates the architectural registers only after every older instruction commits. Where is the result held?
scenarioWhy: The reorder buffer delays retirement so updates to architectural state stay in program order.

definition: Independent instructions from one thread that can be overlapped or issued at the same time.
wrongs: Different threads running at the same time on separate cores.
Disk blocks striped across several drives.
Two cores updating different words of one shared cache line.
why: Instructions that do not depend on each other can occupy multiple functional units or pipeline stages together.
example: An address calculation and an unrelated floating-point multiply from the same thread issue in one cycle.
scenario: Two instructions in one thread have no data dependence and issue together to different units. Which parallelism is being used?
scenarioWhy: The independent work comes from one instruction stream rather than from separate threads.

definition: The lines that carry the address of the memory location or device register being accessed.
wrongs: The lines that carry the data value being read or written.
The lines that carry read, write, and interrupt commands.
The lines that carry only cache-coherence state.
why: Memory and devices decode this address to select which location the transfer refers to.
example: A load drives 0x2000 onto the address lines so the DRAM selects that word.
scenario: During a read, the CPU drives the location to be read while other lines will carry the returned word. Which bus carries the location?
scenarioWhy: The selected location is an address, so it travels on the address bus.

definition: The lines that carry the value being read or written between the CPU, memory, and devices.
wrongs: The lines that carry only the address of the selected location.
The lines that carry only read and write commands.
The bypass wires that forward an ALU result inside one core.
why: After a location is selected, the payload of the transfer moves on the data lines.
example: A store of the value 42 drives 42 on the data lines while the address lines select the destination word.
scenario: The address is already driven, and the word being stored now travels toward DRAM. Which bus carries that word?
scenarioWhy: The value being written is data, so it is transferred on the data bus.

definition: The lines that carry command and timing signals such as read, write, and interrupt request.
wrongs: The lines that carry the memory address.
The lines that carry the data word being transferred.
The lines that carry parity bits among RAID disks.
why: A device must be told whether the cycle is a read or a write and when the address and data are valid.
example: Asserting the memory-write strobe tells DRAM to store the data-bus value at the addressed location.
scenario: Address and data are already driven, and a separate signal says this cycle is a write. Which bus carries that signal?
scenarioWhy: A read or write command is a control signal, not the address and not the payload.

definition: A disk layout that stripes blocks across drives and keeps no redundant copy, so one drive failure loses the array.
wrongs: A layout that stores a full second copy of every block on another drive.
A layout that stripes data with rotating parity and survives one disk failure.
A layout that keeps two independent parity blocks and survives two disk failures.
why: Striping lets drives transfer in parallel, but there is no mirror or parity from which a lost block can be rebuilt.
example: Even-numbered blocks sit on disk A and odd-numbered blocks on disk B, and loss of either disk destroys the file.
scenario: Two disks stripe a file for speed, and the file is unreadable after either disk fails. Which RAID level is this?
scenarioWhy: Striping without a mirror or parity cannot reconstruct data after a disk is lost.

definition: A disk layout that stores a full copy of every block on a second drive so either drive can supply the data.
wrongs: A layout that stripes blocks and stores no second copy.
A layout that stores parity instead of a complete second copy of each block.
A layout that survives two disk failures by keeping double parity.
why: Mirroring means the surviving disk still holds every block after one drive fails.
example: Each database page is written to both disk A and disk B, and a read may be served by either disk.
scenario: Every block is written to two disks, and the array still serves all data after one disk dies. Which RAID level is this?
scenarioWhy: A complete second copy of every block is mirroring, which is RAID 1.

definition: A disk layout that stripes data and rotates parity across the drives so the array can survive one disk failure.
wrongs: A layout that stripes data with no parity and fails if any one disk fails.
A layout that mirrors every block onto a pair of disks.
A layout with two parity blocks that can survive two disk failures.
why: XOR parity can rebuild one missing block, and rotating that parity avoids a single parity-disk bottleneck.
example: When disk B of a three-disk RAID 5 array fails, its blocks are rebuilt by XORing the surviving data and parity.
scenario: Four disks use rotating parity, keep serving data after one disk fails, and cannot survive a second failure. Which RAID level is this?
scenarioWhy: Single distributed parity tolerates one failure, while tolerance of two failures would be double parity.

definition: A chip that contains two or more complete cores able to run different threads at the same time.
wrongs: A single core that issues several instructions from one thread in one cycle.
A five-stage pipeline inside one core.
A disk controller attached to several drives.
why: Each core has its own execution resources, so separate threads can make progress concurrently.
example: A four-core chip runs a compiler thread and three other threads at the same instant.
scenario: One chip executes four independent threads at once, and each thread has its own register file. Which design is this?
scenarioWhy: Separate cores, each with private registers, execute different threads concurrently.

definition: A speedup bound showing that the serial fraction of a program limits the benefit of more parallel hardware.
wrongs: A claim that doubling the number of cores always doubles the whole program's speed.
A claim that doubling cache capacity always halves the miss rate.
A claim that a parity array always survives two disk failures.
why: The portion that cannot be parallelized still takes the same time no matter how many cores run the rest.
example: When one quarter of the runtime is serial, even unlimited cores cannot speed the program up by more than four times.
scenario: A program spends one fifth of its time in code that cannot be parallelized. With unlimited cores, what maximum speedup does the bound give?
scenarioWhy: The serial fraction is one fifth, so the speedup bound is one divided by that fraction, which equals 5.

definition: The requirement that cores not permanently disagree about the value of one memory location held in private caches.
wrongs: The rules for the order in which writes to different addresses become visible to other cores.
The mapping of virtual pages onto physical frames.
The striping of disk blocks across an array of drives.
why: A write must invalidate or update other cached copies so a later read of that same address cannot keep seeing a stale line.
example: After core 0 writes x, core 1's old cache line for x is invalidated before core 1 reads the new x.
scenario: Two cores cache x, core 0 writes x, and core 1 must not keep its old copy of x indefinitely. Which property requires that?
scenarioWhy: Coherence concerns a single address and forbids another cache from retaining a stale copy forever.

definition: A cache-coherence protocol whose line states are Modified, Exclusive, Shared, and Invalid.
wrongs: A page-replacement policy that keeps four queues of pages.
A disk layout that stores four copies of every block.
A branch predictor that remembers only four history bits.
why: Each state records whether the line is dirty, solely owned, shared and clean, or unusable.
example: A shared line becomes Modified when this core writes it, and other caches receive invalidations.
scenario: A cache line is dirty and this cache alone has the up-to-date copy. Which MESI state is that?
scenarioWhy: Modified means the line is dirty and is not present as a valid copy in any other cache.

definition: The model that states which orders of loads and stores to memory may become visible to other processors.
wrongs: The protocol that only keeps the cached copies of a single address from diverging forever.
The translation of one process's virtual addresses into physical frames.
The prediction of which instruction follows a branch.
why: Coherence covers one location, while consistency covers how accesses to different locations may be reordered as others observe them.
example: Under a relaxed model, another core can observe a write to y before it observes an earlier write to x from the same core.
scenario: A core writes x and then y, and another core may see the new y while still seeing the old x. What decides whether that order is allowed?
scenarioWrongs: The coherence protocol for one address only
scenarioWhy: Consistency rules govern the observable order of accesses to different addresses.

definition: A model whose result matches some single interleaving that preserves each core's program order.
wrongs: A model that allows one core's writes to become visible to others out of program order.
A cache policy that updates memory only when a dirty line is evicted.
A scheduler that always runs the highest-priority ready task.
why: All cores agree on one total order, and each core's own accesses appear in that order as the program issued them.
example: If one core writes data and then a flag, no other core can observe the new flag together with the old data.
scenario: Core 0 writes data before a flag, and every core that sees the new flag is guaranteed to see the new data, with no extra fence. Which model provides that guarantee?
scenarioWhy: Program order is preserved in one global interleaving, so the earlier data write is visible no later than the later flag write.

definition: Extra coherence traffic caused when cores write different data that happen to lie on the same cache line.
wrongs: Two cores writing the same variable, which truly must be kept coherent.
Two blocks that collide in a direct-mapped cache inside one core.
Two processes mapping the same virtual page with the page table.
why: Coherence tracks whole lines, so a write to one word invalidates another core's copy of the neighboring words.
example: Core 0 increments counter A while core 1 increments counter B, and both counters occupy one 64-byte line.
scenario: Two cores update different counters, the program slows down, and moving the counters onto separate lines fixes it. What was the problem?
scenarioWhy: The counters were independent, but they shared a line, so each write invalidated the other core's copy.

definition: A transfer in which a device moves blocks to or from memory without the CPU copying each word.
wrongs: A transfer in which the CPU executes a load or store for every word.
A transfer of page-table entries into the TLB.
A transfer of predicted targets into the branch buffer.
why: The device or its controller becomes bus master, so the CPU can do other work while the block moves.
example: A disk controller writes a 4 KB sector into a RAM buffer and interrupts the CPU only when the sector is complete.
scenario: A network card writes an incoming packet into RAM and interrupts the CPU only after the packet is complete. What moved the bytes?
scenarioWhy: The device wrote memory directly, and the CPU did not copy the bytes with loads and stores.

definition: A scheme in which device registers are read and written with ordinary loads and stores to reserved addresses.
wrongs: A scheme that uses separate input and output instructions and a distinct I/O port space.
A scheme that maps virtual pages to blocks on disk.
A scheme that maps architectural registers to physical registers.
why: Devices decode ranges of the physical address space, so the same load and store paths reach their registers.
example: A store to address 0x40001000 writes a UART transmit register rather than a DRAM location.
scenario: Firmware turns on an LED by storing 1 to a GPIO register at a normal memory address. Which I/O organization is this?
scenarioWhy: The device register is selected by an ordinary address instead of by a separate I/O port instruction.

definition: The choice of which requesting master may drive a shared bus during a given cycle.
wrongs: The choice of which cache line to evict from a set.
The choice of which path to fetch after a branch.
The choice of which disk stores the parity block.
why: Only one master can drive the shared address and data lines at a time, so an arbiter grants the bus.
example: The CPU and a DMA controller both request the memory bus, and the arbiter grants it to the controller first.
scenario: The CPU and a disk controller both need the memory bus in the same cycle. What selects which one may drive it?
scenarioWhy: An arbiter grants the shared bus to one master so two devices do not drive the lines together.
